children.text:
The Ayurvedasūtram, chapters 1-5 [a machine-readable
                    transcription by Zoe Slatoff]
children.translated_text: The <s>Āyurvedasūtram</s>, chapters 1-5 [a machine-readable transcription by Zoe Slatoff]
Chapter 1

Now, therefore, one should learn about the <s>dhātus</s> (bodily tissues), the movements of <s>doṣas</s> (humors) situated in them, the causes of disorders, the beneficial substances, and the substances that promote growth
The undertaking born of the desire for long life serves the purpose of <s>Āyurveda</s> (science of life) and the aims of human life
One should protect that which is the cause of health
Neither excessive indulgence nor excessive affliction of the senses
[These two] cause the increase and decrease of the <s>doṣas</s> (humors)
The symptoms are likewise
And one should counteract that with appropriate remedies
One should maintain freedom from <s>āma</s> (undigested matter)
For <s>āma</s> (undigested matter) is [the root] of all diseases
<s>Brahmā</s> declared it to be the primary cause
The cessation of that is freedom from disease
One who is free from disease regards the self as whole
The sense of 'I' is the doer of action
The one possessing a place is the <s>ahaṃkārī</s> (ego-possessor)
As long as one considers oneself free from disease
That very one enjoys
For the unborn one is the presiding ruler
He enjoys the pleasures of sense objects
Another experiences the fruits of action
He who is the doer is the experiencer of actions
The doer is the embodied one
The disembodied one does not eat food
The body alone is not fit for enjoyment — it is so due to union with the <s>ātman</s> (self)
For the two unborn ones preside
Another eats food
The other does not eat in this way
When the body exists, it is for the sake of enjoyment
The embodied one has eight limbs
The body exists as long as the process of creation continues
Seizure is [characterized by] conflict arising from <s>āma</s>-born disease, its causal factors, mental agitation, fear, and restraint
Those that counteract <s>āma</s>-born disease, causally-produced disease, and disease from other causes are rooted in the causation of unprecedented bodily factors
Pains arising from the absence of <s>doṣa</s> circulation, from the joints of bones, ears, nose, etc. — some are counteracted by surgical instruments

One who illuminates, who has attained the first journey, who has obtained the released <s>amṛta</s> (nectar), who returns, who draws forth the division of <s>yoga</s>, who nourishes the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues), who gratifies the gods — such a one is free from disease and aging
He who knows thus
He attains long life
That itself is the medicine
That itself is the treatment
One should examine the substances to that extent
The <s>rasas</s> (tastes) are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent — they are protective
Sweet, sour, and pungent are the <s>rasas</s> (tastes) to be consumed
Such that the <s>doṣas</s> (humors) remain balanced and such that they promote <s>agni</s> (digestive fire)
Of the six, three are established upon digestion
Bitter becomes sweet upon digestion
Astringent has a sour post-digestive taste
Pungent becomes salty upon digestion
Tastes with reversed sequence cause disorders
<s>Pācaka pitta</s> (digestive fire-humor) digests food
It is likewise born of the heat of the <s>doṣas</s> (humors), <s>dhātus</s> (tissues), and <s>malas</s> (waste products)
It sustains the membrane of the intestine, life-span, and radiance
Due to the obstruction of the stomach by food intake, the membrane gains strength

When the stomach is overfilled, due to the obstruction of the movement of <s>pavana</s> (wind) situated in the stomach by the strength of the membrane, aggravation of <s>anila</s> (wind) indeed occurs
Whatever the nature of the <s>doṣas</s> (humors), such is the fire born of <s>anila</s> (wind) aggravation, and such are the fevers
Burning in the eyes, ears, nose, and head, pain, burning sensation, dryness of the tongue and mouth, the abdomen — blazing, it burns

<s>Anila</s> (wind) fever arises from bodily affliction, obstruction of the waste channels, excessive pressure, movement through the <s>dhātu</s> (tissue) pathways, and displacement of fire from its site by wind, among other causes

A disease with symptoms of both, caused by <s>pavana</s> (wind) and <s>pitta</s>, born from improper taste combinations, produced by indigestion, moving through <s>āma</s> (undigested matter), blood, and <s>rasa</s> (nutrient fluid) <s>dhātus</s> — this is <s>pavana-pitta</s> aggravation fever

A disease with symptoms of both, caused by <s>pavana</s> (wind) and <s>kapha</s> disturbance, born from improper taste combinations, produced by indigestion, moving through flesh and fat <s>dhātus</s> — this is <s>pavana-kapha</s> disorder fever

A disease with symptoms of both, caused by <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s> disturbance, born from improper taste combinations, produced by indigestion, with <s>doṣas</s> moving through bone and marrow <s>dhātus</s> — this is <s>kapha-pitta</s> disorder fever

The qualities of exogenous fevers produced by causes such as mental desire, fear, supernatural beings, physical injury, and time include internal burning, difficulty breathing, cough, intoxication, dizziness, fainting, vomiting, diarrhea, grief, anger, and fear — their counteractants are the remedies for these
The sequence of treatment nourishes the strength of <s>agni</s> (digestive fire) by preventing the aggravation of <s>pavana</s> (wind) and others

Through proper diet, when the <s>doṣas</s> (humors) are diminished and the strength of <s>agni</s> (digestive fire) has arisen, hunger, thirst, appetite, and strength [return]; one who knows the division of strength and time becomes well through emesis, purgation, and [treatment of] breathing disorders, cough, heart disease, irregular fever, and diarrhea
That which is situated in the stomach is the strengthener of all <s>dhātus</s> (tissues)
The membrane, situated there, digests by blazing through <s>samāna anila</s> (equalizing wind)
The impaired <s>grahaṇī</s> (intestinal membrane) is the cause of disease

children.text:
dravadravyairvibhajankālādannaṃ prāṇānilena koṣṭhaṃ gataṃ samānānilena
                        tatsthā kalā jvalayantī pacati
children.translated_text: Separating by means of liquid substances at the proper time, when food has gone to the <s>koṣṭha</s> (gut) by <s>prāṇa anila</s> (vital wind), the membrane situated there, blazing, digests through <s>samāna anila</s> (equalizing wind)
When [the stomach] is empty, <s>vāyu</s> (wind) becomes aggravated
The digestive fire becomes weak
Food that has become sweetened after ingestion removes the aggravation of <s>pavana</s> (wind)
Food flooded by <s>kapha</s> that has gone to the heart, having become sour, destroys the aggravation of <s>pitta</s>
Food that has fallen from the heart, dried by the digestive fire, removes <s>kapha</s> situated in the stomach

children.text:
svādvamlakaṭukāḥ pākyā rasā yathā samadoṣā yathāyathaṃ
                        yogaphaladāyakāḥ
children.translated_text: Sweet, sour, and pungent are the <s>rasas</s> (tastes) to be digested — such that the <s>doṣas</s> remain balanced, they yield results according to their appropriate combinations
Those <s>rasas</s> (tastes) are the causes thereof; the fires born from them nourish the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) produced from them
From <s>rasa</s> (nutrient fluid) comes <s>rakta</s> (blood)
The body is composed of the five elements
Sound is heard through the two <s>sirās</s> (channels) situated within the ear that awaken the quality of sound
<s>Ākāśa</s> (space) has the quality of sound
The skin, born from <s>rasa</s> (nutrient fluid) and <s>asṛk</s> (blood) <s>dhātus</s> (tissues), carries inhalation and exhalation
Wind enveloped by the skin of the seven <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) is born from separation
The fire situated in the eyes, enveloped by fifty-six <s>sirās</s> (channels), digesting food endowed with five forms, being a fire born of wind, perceives its own object
In the form of saliva, separating the varieties beginning with <s>rasa</s> (taste), [one] grasps taste through the tongue
The tongue, supported by two <s>sirās</s> (channels) situated in it, knows all tastes
Twenty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels) originating at the tip of the nose — <s>pṛthivī</s> (earth) makes known twenty-four principles

children.text:
yatsirāvṛtaṃ śarīram | annādbhūtāni jāyante, jātānyannena vardhante,
                        adyate ‘tti ca bhūtāni, tasmādannaṃ taducyate
children.translated_text: The body is pervaded by <s>sirās</s> (channels). From food beings are born; once born, they grow by food; it is eaten and it eats beings — therefore it is called <s>anna</s> (food)
Disorders arising from excess in the nose are perceived at the tip of the nose

children.text:
mātṛjaṃ raktamāṃsamedaḥ, pitṛjaṃ majjāsthiretaḥ, satvarajastamoguṇātmakaṃ
                        śarīram
children.translated_text: From the mother come <s>rakta</s> (blood), <s>māṃsa</s> (flesh), and <s>medas</s> (fat); from the father come <s>majjā</s> (marrow), <s>asthi</s> (bone), and <s>retas</s> (semen); the body is of the nature of the three <s>guṇas</s>: <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>
The body, [endowed with] longevity, health, radiance, strength, and purity, is produced by the quality of <s>sattva</s>
The <s>rasas</s> (tastes) situated in their respective locations, born from those respective elements, nourish the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues)

children.text:
athāta ādibhūtaṃ yaḥ kartā yāvatkṛtestathā tadeva bheṣajaṃ
                        manaḥkāmahṛdgatakaphaśuklādibhirāvṛtaṃ śarīraṃ daśa
children.translated_text: Now, therefore — the primordial element, the one who creates, and the extent of creation, that itself is the medicine; the body is enveloped by mind, desire, <s>kapha</s> that has gone to the heart, <s>śukla</s> (semen) and other [substances] — ten [in number]
Chapter 2
One having two <s>rasas</s> (tastes) whose purpose lacks taste and whose taste lacks purpose — it counteracts <s>anila</s> (wind)
There are six thousand and thirty <s>sirās</s> (channels), thirty <s>śalyas</s> (foreign bodies), two hundred and ten joints, eighty-nine <s>snāyu</s> (sinew) and <s>peśī</s> (muscle) supports

Supported by seven <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) and seven <s>āśayas</s> (receptacles), the sweet <s>rasa</s> (taste) born from the <s>grahaṇī kalā</s> (intestinal membrane) situated in the middle of them removes the aggravation of <s>anila</s> (wind)
The eighth is the <s>garbhāśaya</s> (uterus) in women

children.text:
svaṃ svaṃ svoṣmaṇā sravadrasātmaṃ caujaḥ | svaṃ svaṃ svasya svayameva
                        heturbhavati
children.translated_text: Each one, through its own heat, produces <s>ojas</s> (vital essence) from the flowing <s>rasa</s> (nutrient fluid); each one itself becomes the cause of its own [sustenance]
The limbs are: head, hands, feet, sides, back, thighs, abdomen, shanks, penis, perineum, and anus
Likewise the [sense organs]: ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose
Three by three <s>sirās</s> (channels) with openings and internal supports [are found in each]; in the feet there are thirty-four <s>sirās</s> with openings and internal supports
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) situated in the feet, which generates the 'a' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the knees, which generates the 'i' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the thigh region, of the nature of the 'u' sound, is enveloped by twenty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the hip region, which generates the 'ṛ' sound, is enveloped by twenty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the hip region, which generates the 'lṛ' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the waist region, which generates the 'e' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the side of the generative region, which generates the 'ai' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the groin region, which generates the 'o' sound, is enveloped by twelve <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the generative region, which generates the 'au' sound, is enveloped by two <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The [plexus] in the penile region, which generates the 'ga' and 'gha' sounds, is enveloped by sixty-three <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the back region, which causes the utterance of the 'ṅa' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the back region, which causes the utterance of the 'ṅa' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the side thereof, which produces the 'ca' and 'cha' sounds, is enveloped by fourteen <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) of the <s>jaṭharānala</s> (abdominal fire), which causes the utterance of the 'ja' and 'jha' sounds, is enveloped by fourteen <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the navel region, which produces the 'ña' sound, is enveloped by twenty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the navel region, which produces the 'ṭa' and 'ṭha' sounds, is enveloped by thirty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The [plexus] at the side of the hair-line, which causes the 'ḍa' and 'ḍha' sounds, is enveloped by twenty-two <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>hṛt-kamala</s> (heart-lotus), which is the basis of the 'ṇa' sound, is enveloped by thirty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the two breasts, which produces the 'ta' and 'tha' sounds, is enveloped by fifty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the throat region, which produces the 'da' and 'dha' sounds, is enveloped by fifty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the neck, which produces the 'na' sound, is enveloped by sixteen <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the arms, which produces the 'pa' and 'pha' sounds, is enveloped by sixteen <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the forearm region, which generates the 'ba' and 'bha' sounds, is enveloped by fifty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the hands, which causes the utterance of the 'ma' sound and makes known the meaning of all words, is enveloped by fifty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) of taste-binding, which makes known the 'ya' sound, is enveloped by two <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the lips, which produces the 'ra' sound, is enveloped by sixteen <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The [plexus] situated in the region of the lord of speech, which generates the 'la' sound, is enveloped by two <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the tip of the nose, which produces the 'va' sound, is enveloped by thirty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) carrying smell, which makes known the 'śa' sound, is enveloped by two <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the two palates, which produces the 'ṣa' sound, is each enveloped by a single <s>sirā</s> (channel)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the eye region, which makes known the 'sa' sound, is enveloped by fifty-four <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the temple region, which produces the 'ha' sound, is enveloped by two <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the outer corner of the eye region, which produces the 'ḷa' sound, is enveloped by two <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) in the region of the row of teeth, which makes known the 'kṣa' sound, is enveloped by thirty <s>sirās</s> (channels)
The <s>padma</s> (plexus) at the cheeks, which produces the <s>repha</s> (the 'ra' sound), has the deity of the 'ra' sound
Sound born from the movement of <s>doṣas</s> in the <s>sirās</s> (channels) reaches the ears
<s>Sirās</s> (channels) that are empty, overly full, or excessively filled should not be pierced
Those <s>sirās</s> (channels) that go to the <s>marma</s> (vital points) and <s>āśayas</s> (receptacles) are empty
Having understood the method of separating blood in the <s>sirās</s> (channels), one should release it
The parents should be such — free from pain in their limbs
From earthly substances that are the cause of pure receptacles, pure <s>doṣas</s> (humors), pure digestive fire, and pure sense faculties, offspring are born
The union of <s>śukra</s> (semen) and <s>śoṇita</s> (menstrual blood) is the womb
In the womb, the unborn one manifested, impelled by divine ordinance
One assumes a form corresponding to the food consumed
<s>Rasas</s> (tastes) that grant freedom from disease are the counteractants
As long as possible, one should nourish the maternal [contribution] from the <s>rasas</s> (tastes) consumed
When the father's semen predominates, a son is born
When the mother's blood predominates, a daughter is born
Where the two are equal, a <s>ṣaṇḍa</s> (eunuch) is born
The unborn one is born in various ways
One should bathe on the fourth day
Having been purified, she should go to her husband
Those desiring offspring should make effort in intercourse to that extent, for that is the cause

children.text:
dvicatuḥṣaṣṭhāṣṭadaśadvādaśe ‘hani jātāh putrāḥ taditare ‘hani jātāḥ
                        putrikāḥ
children.translated_text: Sons are born on the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth days; daughters are born on the other days
In the first menstrual period, the nourishing [substance] is the counteractant

children.text:
tadūrdhve ṛtau śoṣakaṃ tadanantaramapi śoṣakarasāḥ garbhābhivardhakā
                        yāvatkālopayogyāḥ
children.translated_text: After that, during the fertile period, the drying [substance] and thereafter also the drying <s>rasas</s> (tastes) promote the growth of the embryo, being suitable for the time
In the first, second, and third months, sweet <s>rasas</s> (tastes) that remove <s>pavana</s> (wind) are the counteractants
In the fourth, fifth, and sixth months, sour <s>rasas</s> (tastes) that remove <s>pitta</s> are the counteractants
In the sixth, eighth, and ninth months, pungent <s>rasas</s> (tastes) that dry <s>kapha</s> are the promoters
The disorder should be counteracted
The disorder arising from the increase of <s>āma</s> (undigested matter) is the cause of all diseases
The appropriate substance at the appropriate time, in the appropriate domain, counteracts the appropriate [disorders]
That which counteracts is the medicine
It is caused by the three <s>doṣas</s> (humors)
For all living beings, maintaining freedom from <s>āma</s> (undigested matter) is the counteractant
A substance that promotes <s>vahni</s> (digestive fire), and one that strengthens the body and promotes the <s>jaṭharānala</s> (abdominal fire)
Substances suitable for oleation for their respective purposes are the promoters
That which is made of purified <s>sneha</s> (oil/fat) is the counteractant
The joining of limb to limb, anointing of limbs, and the separation of limbs shine forth
The fire born within the pregnant woman is produced by the consumption of ghee by the pregnant woman
For those that give birth to sky-moving [creatures], together with ghee, in the body of birds
The ascending of those who travel the paths of the sky
From the consumption of food soaked in ghee, <s>vāyu</s> (wind) sustains radiance and <s>retas</s> (reproductive fluid)
It increases through the use of suitable substances.
The seasons flourish from it.
From food, beings are born.
Once born, they grow by food.
It is eaten and it eats beings.
Therefore it is called <s>anna</s> (food), thus it is said.
One should give food drenched in <s>ghṛta</s> (clarified butter) to a pregnant woman.
Therefore, offspring are born from those who nourish the <s>dhātus</s> (bodily tissues) to their full capacity in their own limbs.
That which dries and nourishes is the substance; therein lies the medicine.
Thus there is progressive increase month by month.
As long as there is growth, therein the medicines apply.
Those to be nourished are nourished by <s>sarpiṣ</s> (ghee).
At the time of nourishing, drying agents should not be used.
The six <s>rasas</s> (tastes) nourish the seven <s>dhātus</s> (tissues).
<s>Rasa</s> (chyle) indeed becomes <s>asṛk</s> (blood).
<s>Rasa</s> (essence) indeed is He.
Chapter 3
Now, the teaching of <s>yoga</s> (union).
<s>Yoga</s> is the transformation of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) through the cognition directed inward toward the knowledge between <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self).
From the excess of <s>rajas</s> (activity), instability arises; when directed outward, it becomes the cause of pleasure and pain.
From the excess of <s>tamas</s> (inertia), due to ignorance of what should and should not be done, one becomes deluded, governed by anger and other afflictions.
From the rise of <s>sattva</s> (purity), happiness arises.
From eating food of sweet taste, the cause of <s>sāttvika</s> (pure) qualities follows.
Eating soured food produces <s>rājasa</s> (passionate) qualities.
Pungent substances are the cause of <s>tamas</s> (inertia) quality.
For the seeker of liberation, sweetness is prescribed.
From eating sour taste, only one kind of pleasure is experienced.

The erroneous knowledge pertaining to the defect arising from the obstruction of blood caused by excess of drying substances, and the movement of wind and fire through the channels — this is the cause of obstruction to valid cognition.

That perception arises from eating substances having bitter and pungent tastes.

From the rise of <s>sattva</s> born of the transformation of sweet taste, the designation 'this is that one' arises.
<s>Abhyāsa</s> (practice) is the cessation of contact with other sense objects, internally regulated.
<s>Vairāgya</s> (dispassion) is the repeated re-engagement arising from the enthusiasm of flow, born of detachment from sense objects.
The designations of mastery over craving for objects seen and heard are likewise.

The restraint of <s>Prāṇa</s>, <s>Apāna</s>, <s>Vyāna</s>, <s>Udāna</s>, and <s>Samāna</s> winds circulating through the tissue-channels and veins becomes the cause of confusion as long as it persists.

children.text:
tatsaṃyogajātadhātavaḥ pravartakāh (yāṃ kāmayeta duhitaraṃ priyā syaditi |
                        tāṃ niṣṭhāya dadyāt | priyaiva bhavati | sa na tu punarāgacchati)
children.translated_text: The <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) born from that union are the promoters. (Whichever daughter one desires to be beloved — having established her, one should give her away; she becomes beloved indeed. He does not return again.)
Woman and man are portions of the self, by the desire to create from the undivided form.
<s>Prakṛti</s> (nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (spirit) are remembered as the parents.
<s>Yoga</s> practice is the repeated re-engagement with enthusiasm in one's own true nature, which is obscured by mental activities.
The stages in <s>yoga</s> and other practices arise from repeated observation born of extraordinary devotion.
Having established her, one should give her away.
She becomes beloved indeed.
One does not return here again.
<s>Vairāgya</s> (dispassion) is the knowledge that the enjoyments of objects pertaining to this world and the next are perishable.
<s>Vairāgya</s> (dispassion) is that which is caused by the uninterrupted bliss of knowledge, which is of the nature of bliss free from sense objects.
Therefore, the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) are the supports for the stages of their diseases.
The body is the abode of experience.
That supreme dispassion toward the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) arises from the knowledge of the Supreme <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self).
As long as contemplation producing the impression of meaning regarding sense-object knowledge is practiced, it is <s>savitarka</s> (with deliberation).
The practice of contemplation dependent upon objects qualified by the properties of the inner instrument, with reference to space and time, is <s>savicāra</s> (with reflection).
In this, the manifestation of the property alone, qualified by space, time, and attribute, is <s>nirvicāra</s> (without reflection).
That which pertains to the power of consciousness through the overflow of the manifestation of bliss is <s>ānanda</s> (bliss).
In this, <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) is remembered as that which pertains only to the bare existence of the object to be grasped as real.
Sweet taste, filling, with an upsurge like undisturbed honey-flow through the wind moving in <s>rasa</s> (chyle) and <s>asṛk</s> (blood), resides in the thumb.
The <s>kalā</s> (potency) situated there, causing the ten-petaled lotus to bloom, moves forth.
The <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self), the size of a thumb, resides in the thumb.
<s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) bears the body of the entire universe.
The <s>Mūlādhāra</s> (root support) is the primordial source, the nourisher of all <s>dhātus</s> (tissues).
The wind moving through the channel-paths draws the nectar situated in the head-lotus and irrigates it.
It is likewise the primordial source of the branches and shoots of the body.
The nectar flowing through the channel-paths to the respective presiding letters and deities of each center is the nourisher.
At the base of that lotus of the feet, the river flows.
By the wind moving through the channel-paths running along the flesh, filling the <s>kalās</s> (potencies), one should irrigate with nectar.
There exist channels running along the flesh.
The foot-lotus has its root in two thousand channel-branches.
The body is composed of the seven <s>dhātus</s> (tissues).
Chapter 4
Through the practice of <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) attained by the flow of nectar going and coming, the proximity of <s>yoga</s> is achieved.
That <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) which is near is called intense union.
<s>Saṃvega</s> (spiritual urgency) is the cause of action; it is a firmly established impression.
For those who possess varieties of means of going and coming, the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) is near.
From the mild, medium, and intense degrees, there arises distinction.
Mild, medium, and intense — these are the varieties of means.
Mild union, medium union, and intense union.
By threefold division of the wind, there arise nine types of <s>yogins</s> (practitioners).
The fifteen-petaled lotus situated in the region of the calves, supported by a thousand channels, is located in the fifty <s>marmas</s> (vital points).
<s>Samādhi</s> (absorption) is the union of the wind that assists the impressions of going and coming.
The body is the seat of actions impelled by <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), and the seat of actions that promote what is beneficial and harmful as their purpose.
It is of the nature of movement, governed by the wind moving through the channels impelled by the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) generated from the intake of pure <s>rasa</s> (food-essence).
It moves by the force of the transformation brought about by the flow of nourishing nectar to the calf-lotus.

<s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) is a special <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self) untouched by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s> (actions), and their fruition and residue — the promoter of the <s>rasa</s> (essence) through the union of wind born from salty taste.
The eighteen-petaled lotus supported by three hundred channels along the passage of the streams is the seat of the movement of perception going and coming.
Filling by means of the wind-channel born of sweet, sour, and salty tastes, it moves in the domain of the hip-lotus.
From eating substances that are sweet in taste but lacking in flavor, due to indigestion, abdominal disease arises from the increase of <s>āma</s> (undigested toxin) and fluid.
A purgative substance having sweet taste is the medicine therein.
One should purge very gradually.
The course of treatment is to nourish the strength of <s>agni</s> (digestive fire) without aggravating the wind and other humors.

From eating flavorless substances, due to indigestion, from the obstruction of wind situated in the channel-paths, from the excessive flow of channel-fluid, due to indigestion, abdominal disease arises from the increase of <s>āma</s> (toxin) and fluid.

Roughness, excessive cold, lightness, excessive pain, loss of appetite, discoloration, tastelessness in the mouth, drowsiness, fainting, burning, confusion, thirst, fever, diarrhea, and yellowness of the body — caused by the aggravation of wind — are the causes of <s>pitta</s> (bile) aggravation and abdominal disease.

Dyspnea, cough, confusion, burning sensation, dimness of vision, graying of skin and hair, thinning of reproductive tissue — the <s>rasa</s> (fluid) born from the tissue-channels produces <s>kapha</s> (phlegm); <s>kapha</s> creates more <s>kapha</s>.

The abdominal disease of <s>vāta</s> (wind) and <s>pitta</s> (bile), afflicted by the symptoms of both, following two or three <s>rasas</s> (tastes) that generate the aggravation of wind and bile, should be recognized.

The abdominal disease of <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) and <s>pitta</s> (bile), marked by the respective symptoms, following two or three <s>rasas</s> (tastes) that generate the aggravation of phlegm and bile, should be recognized. The abdominal disease of <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s> (wind), following two or three tastes with symptoms of both, should be known. The abdominal disease involving aggravation of <s>pavana</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>kapha</s> (phlegm), following two or three tastes that generate disorders of <s>rasa</s> (chyle), <s>asṛk</s> (blood), <s>māṃsa</s> (flesh), and <s>medas</s> (fat), marked by respective symptoms, is difficult to cure.
The abdominal disease of the spleen generated by worms is likewise.

From eating substances having pungent, sour, and salty tastes, due to obstruction of the waste-passage, from the aggravation of wind that fills upward toward the heart through the openings of those channels, there arise pallor, swelling, spreading skin disease, and pain.

Confusion, vomiting, excessive thirst, retching, thirst, fainting, internal burning, spasms of the body, loss of appetite, and pallor — these are the symptoms of <s>pitta</s>-type pallor and swelling. Excessive pain in the feet, knees, calves, thighs, hips, back, groin, and sides, diarrhea, roughness, excessive cold, and spasms of the whole body — these are the symptoms of <s>pavana</s> (wind)-type pallor and swelling.
Dyspnea, cough, pain in the nose, eyes, eyelashes, ears, cheeks, and teeth, nasal congestion, and piercing headache — these are the symptoms of pallor, swelling, and spreading skin disease.
They corrupt the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) like one afflicted by external poison.

From the obstruction of the movement of <s>vāta</s> (wind) born of the combination of wind, bile, and flavorless substances, from the corruption of <s>rasa</s> (chyle) and <s>asṛk</s> (blood) tissues, graying of the skin and hair becomes the cause of pallor disease.

The poisonous essence of undigested <s>pitta</s> (bile) situated in the heart, which dries the foot-lotus, through the combination of thirty-four channels that awaken the syllables, from the obstruction of the nectar-flow, wind-born diseases increase.
The grasping of the poisonous bile-essence by the six inner supporting channels with openings that awaken the syllables, sustained by the meager nectar-flow, is the cause of wind aggravation.

The unity of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness) comes about.
That in which there is a predominance of earthly constituents and which is perceived as essential — that possesses the quality of <s>pārthiva</s> (earthly) essence.
That which removes a single <s>doṣa</s> (humor) to that extent is of single essence.
That in which the perception of <s>svādu rasa</s> (sweet taste) arises from a predominance of watery constituents — that is of that essence.

A substance having taste, to the extent that it perceives a predominant form arising from a surplus of fiery constituents — that is of that essence.

<s>Tikta</s> (bitter), <s>uṣaṇa</s> (pungent), and <s>kaṣāya</s> (astringent) <s>rasas</s> (tastes) bestow <s>rasa</s> (plasma), <s>asṛk</s> (blood), <s>māṃsa</s> (muscle), <s>medas</s> (fat), and <s>bala</s> (strength).

Chapter 5

children.text:
nābheradhastādūrdhvaṃ hṛdi sthitavātapittakaphadoṣāssamastā asamastā
                        asamagrā anyonyaṃ te āmayotpādakāḥ
children.translated_text: The <s>doṣas</s> (humors) — <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) — situated from below the navel upward in the heart, whether complete, incomplete, or partial, mutually cause disease.
Whichever <s>rasas</s> (tastes) are situated wherever, the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) born and arisen from them nourish those <s>dhātus</s>.
A substance with two <s>rasas</s> (tastes), deficient in a half-rasa, and possessing a diminished taste, removes <s>anila</s> (wind).
<s>Madhura</s> (sweet) and excessively sweet tastes, in sequence, destroy <s>vāta</s> (wind) and <s>pitta</s> (bile) but produce <s>kapha</s> (phlegm).
<s>Āmla</s> (sour) and excessively sour tastes likewise.
<s>Lavaṇa</s> (salty taste) destroys <s>pavana</s> (wind); it causes <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) and <s>pitta</s> (bile).
Deficient or excessive <s>lavaṇa rasa</s> (salty taste) destroys <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) and <s>pavana</s> (wind) but produces <s>pitta</s> (bile).
<s>Tikta</s> (bitter taste) destroys <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) and <s>pitta</s> (bile) but produces <s>māruta</s> (wind).
<s>Kaṭu</s> (pungent taste) destroys <s>kapha</s> (phlegm); it causes <s>vāta</s> (wind) and <s>pitta</s> (bile).
<s>Kaṭuka</s> (pungent) and excessively pungent tastes destroy <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) and <s>anila</s> (wind) but produce <s>pitta</s> (bile).

children.text:
kaṣāyaḥ kaphapittaṃ hanti | mārutaṃ kurute | hīnādhikakaṣāyaḥ kaphamārutaṃ
                        hanti | pittaṃ kurute
children.translated_text: <s>Kaṣāya</s> (astringent taste) destroys <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) and <s>pitta</s> (bile) but produces <s>māruta</s> (wind); deficient or excessive <s>kaṣāya</s> (astringent) destroys <s>kapha</s> (phlegm) and <s>māruta</s> (wind) but produces <s>pitta</s> (bile).

In regard to the <s>doṣas</s> (humors), a single <s>rasa</s> (taste) and the like, being of a nature contrary to the three-<s>doṣa</s> affliction caused by other factors, serves as the remover to that extent.
Substances possessing the essence of <s>rasa</s> (taste) and other qualities remove all diseases.
That which is the essence nourishing the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) without disturbing the <s>doṣas</s> (humors).

children.text:
pakvāmāśayagāḥ pavanādyāḥ svādukaṣāyakaṭukaistiktāmlalavaṇaiḥ

                        pravardhante
children.translated_text: The <s>pavana</s> (wind) and other <s>doṣas</s> (humors) situated in the <s>pakvāśaya</s> (colon) and <s>āmāśaya</s> (stomach) are treated with various substances possessing the qualities of retention and expulsion, suitable for digestion over time — sweet, astringent, pungent, bitter, sour, and salty.

children.text:
bhūguṇau gurumandau | snigdhahimāvāpaḥ | ślakṣṇasāndratarāgneḥ |
                        mṛdusthitā gurumārutaḥ | sukṣmaviśadā viyataḥ | viruddhaviṣayakāḥ
                        pratikārakāḥ | deśadehakāladravyakarmaṇāṃ yathāyogo yāvadrogapātakaḥ
children.translated_text: The qualities of <s>bhū</s> (earth) are heavy and slow; <s>āpas</s> (water) is unctuous and cool; <s>agni</s> (fire) is smooth and dense; <s>māruta</s> (wind) is soft, stable, and heavy; <s>viyat</s> (space) is subtle and clear; the specific properties are accordingly established.
Those who are healthy and unhealthy, having diseases with <s>āma</s> (undigested toxins) and without, with <s>doṣas</s> (humors) and without <s>doṣas</s>.
The appropriate application of place, time, substance, and action in the body, to the extent that it destroys the disease.

A disease arising from improper digestion of tasteless and irregular substances, traveling through the pathway of two <s>doṣas</s> (humors) and one type of <s>dhātu</s> (tissue), is of two <s>doṣas</s>.
A disease that digests the final <s>rasa</s> (taste) involves all three <s>doṣas</s> (humors).
Digestion up to the point of removing the <s>doṣas</s> (humors) is beyond deliberation.
The time of <s>doṣa</s> (humor) digestion depends upon the purification of the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues).
From the ascending of contrary <s>rasas</s> (tastes) through the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) to the extent that there is one <s>dhātu</s> affected.

<s>Jvara</s> (fever) arises with <s>āma</s> (toxins) — when one is overpowered by an excess of <s>doṣa</s> (humor) arising from undigested <s>rasa</s> (taste), tastelessness, excess, and contrary tastes, displaced from one's natural state, blazing outwardly.
The time of <s>doṣa</s> (humor) digestion depends on the purification of the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) through digestion of irregular taste, tastelessness, and similar factors.
Diseases situated in one or two <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) are easily curable.

Diseases arising from two <s>doṣas</s> (humors), spreading through two <s>rasas</s> (tastes), traversing <s>māṃsa</s> (muscle) and <s>medas</s> (fat), with the digestion of one predominant <s>doṣa</s> based on <s>rasa</s> (taste), are difficult to cure.
Likewise those arising from mutual <s>doṣas</s> (humors).
Diseases arising from more than two <s>rasas</s> (tastes), involving three <s>doṣas</s> (humors), and conforming to the nature of <s>rasa</s> (taste) — these are incurable.
Similarly, those situated in a single <s>dhātu</s> (tissue) are also incurable.
Without <s>doṣa</s> (humor), with <s>doṣa</s>, with balanced <s>doṣa</s> — with pain or painless.
Those three <s>doṣas</s> (humors) are the causes, and there are seven <s>dhātus</s> (tissues).
With <s>anila</s> (wind) or without, with excess <s>anila</s>, characterized by the dryness and lightness of <s>anila</s> (wind), it travels through <s>rasa</s> (plasma) and <s>asṛk</s> (blood).
From the seat of <s>pitta</s> (bile), dependent on it, <s>pitta</s> following along <s>māṃsa</s> (muscle) and <s>medas</s> (fat) softens the bones.
Mild warmth and other qualities of balanced and excess <s>doṣas</s> (humors), diminished or increased, are situated in bone, marrow, and fat.

Those that follow the flow of <s>dhātu</s> (tissue) and <s>rasa</s> (taste) without disturbing the <s>doṣas</s> (humors), digesting the final <s>dhātu</s> through <s>rasa</s> digestion — these cause the spreading through the last <s>dhātu</s>.

From the cooking of contrary <s>rasas</s> (tastes) combined with the digestion of balanced <s>rasa</s> through the fire that is the cause of the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) arising from previously existing substances — reversal occurs.
The first of the six <s>kamalas</s> (lotuses) is the <s>Mūlādhāra</s> (root support center).
The <s>amṛta</s> (nectar) arriving through the flow filled by <s>Iḍā</s> and <s>Piṅgalā</s> with wind sprinkles it.
It grows through the regions of the back, thighs, abdomen, calves, penis, and genitals.
Situated below the navel, originating from <s>Kuṇḍalī</s> (the coiled one), the hundred-petalled <s>padma</s> (lotus) enveloped by five thousand <s>sirās</s> (channels) — that lotus is born.
It shines as the furnace of the <s>jaṭharāgni</s> (digestive fire).
Stimulating <s>madhura rasa</s> (sweet taste), it shines with its own radiance in the place of <s>śukra dhātu</s> (reproductive tissue).
Digesting <s>āmla rasa</s> (sour taste), it shines with its own radiance in the place of the great <s>dhātu</s> (tissue).
Digesting <s>lavaṇa rasa</s> (salty taste), it shines with its own radiance in the place of <s>asthi dhātu</s> (bone tissue).
Digesting <s>tikta rasa</s> (bitter taste), it shines with its own radiance in the place of <s>medo dhātu</s> (fat tissue).
Digesting <s>ūṣaṇa rasa</s> (pungent taste), it shines with its own radiance in the place of <s>māṃsa dhātu</s> (muscle tissue).
Digesting <s>kaṣāya rasa</s> (astringent taste), it shines with its own radiance in the place of <s>rasa</s> (plasma) and <s>asṛk dhātu</s> (blood tissue).
The thumb-sized petal, which is the basis of all <s>rasas</s> (tastes), situated upon the <s>nābhi padma</s> (navel lotus), a triangular lotus is born.
From that, the body is born; from that, the limbs shine forth in the body.
The <s>amṛta</s> (nectar) born from it nourishes it.
It is immovable, unborn, and the object of the mind.
Knowledge of that is the highest aim of human life.
The consumption of <s>sāttvika</s> (pure) substances awakens that knowledge.
From the intake of other substances, that does not shine forth.
<s>Rajas</s> (passion) and <s>tamas</s> (inertia) are the two <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) that obstruct self-knowledge.
The body is the cause of all purposes.
That unborn one sees equally.
It consumes all food.
The <s>rasas</s> (tastes) that nourish it, and the branches, fruits, and trunks that nourish those branches.
One should observe the transformation of <s>rasa</s> (taste) through food taken in the morning and forenoon.
One whose receptacles are purified through the proper discharge of feces and urine.
The receptacles of a healthy person accomplish the welfare of the entire body.
The embodied being is either a receptacle of <s>rasa</s> (taste), a receptacle with receptacles, or a receptacle of all.
Fifty-six <s>vasumatī kalās</s> (earthly phases) shine in the heart region.
Fifty radiances, born arising from the navel, shine forth distinctly.
Above that, in the fire, sixty-two rays shine forth.
Fifty-four radiances resting in wind proceed in the belly.
Above that, sixty-two radiances situated in space shine forth.
In the mind located in the middle of the ears, eyes, and nose, the rays open.
Above that, in the <s>Sahasrāra padma</s> (thousand-petalled lotus) situated within the body, the dual form of white shines forth.
From earth to mind, there are six seasons.
The six <s>rasas</s> (tastes), being balanced tastes, are in the form of <s>kalās</s> (phases), called <s>kalās</s>, and are perceived every day.
The <s>kalās</s> (phases) of earth and water nourish in their portions.
The waters are nourished by fire.
From wind comes fire.
From fire comes space.
Next comes the mind.
The mind is called the soul of the age.
The body is enveloped by these.
The six categories of substances, being of the nature of six <s>rasas</s> (tastes), have their respective substance-forms — thus is the teaching.
Having tasted each <s>rasa</s> (taste), the dispassionate mind experiences one thing through another.
Of oneself, by oneself, one who knows thus.
Departing from those worlds, one approaches this self made of bliss.
One approaches this self made of knowledge.
One approaches this self made of mind.
Wandering through these worlds in a form desired, one sits singing this <s>Sāma</s> (chant).
The fire becomes that which has rays upward, downward, and sideways.
That <s>Virāṭ Puruṣa</s> (cosmic being) at the tip of the branches consumes all.
The protection of the nameless is the cause of freedom from disease.
That which nourishes the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues) is the cause of bliss.
Knowledge of <s>rasa</s> (taste) substances is the cause of bliss.
Knowledge of the true nature of the self, preceded by knowledge of the mutual combination of those substances, is the cause of bliss.
The totality of knowledge, preceded by the self, mind, and sense objects, becomes the support for knowledge of each respective object.
The removal of disease and sin establishes and sustains that which has a support.
That which is governed by both of them, which grants fearlessness, which supports the entire body — that is the characteristic of the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues).

children.text:
ivartyanivartakaviṣayavidhiṃ jñātvā viṣaye napramattaṃ
                        sādhyāsādhyavidhiniṣedhajñānapūrvikā kāryā cikitsā
children.translated_text: Having understood the rule regarding reversible and irreversible conditions, one who is not careless regarding sense objects — treatment should be performed preceded by knowledge of what is curable and incurable, and what is prescribed and prohibited.
For each individual bodily substance, there is a specific medicine.
The quality born of <s>pṛthivī</s> (earth), in a substance with sour taste and one without taste, causes desiccation and nourishment respectively.
The quality born of <s>ap</s> (water), in a substance whose taste has departed and one without taste, causes desiccation and nourishment respectively.
Born of <s>tejas</s> (fire) element — the pungent <s>rasa</s> (taste) containing hidden salty and pungent tastes causes desiccation and nourishment in water and wind respectively.

Born of <s>pavana bhūta</s> (wind element), the substance suitable for contact, pervaded by all <s>rasas</s> (tastes), with blood-<s>rasa</s> scattered from the extracted taste — it removes all <s>doṣas</s> (humors).

Born of <s>gagana bhūta</s> (space element), the <s>kaṣāya rasa</s> (astringent taste) dependent on space, the bitter taste established in the earth-nature of its shadow, along with wind and fire dependent on <s>anila</s> (wind) — to the extent they remove diseases situated in all <s>doṣas</s> (humors).
Through the intake of substances that nourish the <s>dhātus</s> (tissues), the respective diseases are removed.
The striking of sense objects against the self is the cause of excess <s>māruta</s> (wind).
Diseases born from non-intake and from injury — for diseases caused by injury to non-intake, the cessation of the irreversible occurs through non-intake.
Diseases born from injury are difficult to cure.
Those that destroy the <s>sirās</s> (channels) destroy the body.
From affliction at the final time, it is born from injury.
This is the cause of discourse on <s>kṣaya</s> (wasting), <s>arśas</s> (hemorrhoids), <s>gulma</s> (abdominal tumors), and eye diseases.
From the desiccation of the body and the digestion of the body, the essence of the body flows out excessively.
<s>Svādu rasa</s> (sweet taste) nourishes <s>śukra</s> (reproductive tissue).
<s>Svādu rasa</s> (sweet taste) when tasteless desiccates <s>śukra</s> (reproductive tissue).
<s>Amla rasa</s> (sour taste) promotes <s>majjā</s> (marrow).
<s>Amla rasa</s> (sour taste) when tasteless causes deficiency of <s>majjā</s> (marrow).
